name: Lookism

lead: Lookism means prejudice against people seen as unattractive, or assuming things about someone from how they look. In looksmaxxing it is the reason many men give for working on their looks: people are treated differently based on appearance, so improving yours changes how others respond.

Researchers point to stereotypes that attractive people are more capable or kind, and to employers and others acting on those impressions. Field experiments with fictitious résumés have found callback differences in several countries, and studies report appearance effects on pay and perceived health-care treatment, though size varies by setting.

paras: People use the idea as motivation, picking areas such as grooming, fitness, skin, clothing or height presentation to work on. Forum culture built around the term shares tips and rates progress.

Studies link perceived appearance discrimination with poorer self-rated health, and one analysis of a looksmaxxing forum describes health harms from its appearance-focused norms. Legal protection against appearance discrimination is rare.

social.title: Should We Do More to Fight Lookism?
The Eye of the Beholder: Appearance Discrimination in the Workplace

chain: Different treatment in hiring and dating
angle.text: Lookism is the term for judging people by appearance, and it is the reason many men give for working on their looks: better presentation changes how people respond in hiring, dating and elsewhere. Sociology and economics research reports real but variable attractiveness effects.

lead: Lookism is prejudice or discrimination against people judged physically unattractive, and also the tendency to infer someone's abilities or character from their appearance. It is studied in sociology, economics and psychology and is discussed in hiring, dating, politics and healthcare. [1]

The word is also core vocabulary in looksmaxxing communities, where it is often used to describe the belief that appearance largely determines how people are treated, and as a name for the forum culture built around that belief. Some of the early looksmaxxing forums used the word in their names. [2][3]

Published research reports measurable appearance effects in callbacks for jobs, in wages and in perceived health-care treatment, though researchers disagree about how large these effects are in different settings and whether they amount to injustice. Peer-reviewed work has also begun to examine looksmaxxing forums themselves as a health-relevant online community. [1][4][5]

sections.h: Definition and origin of the term
paras: Wikipedia describes lookism as prejudice against people considered unattractive, or the judging of intelligence or ability by appearance. The article says the term grew in popularity in the 1970s in the fat acceptance movement, and cites a 1978 Washington Post article attributing the coinage to fat people describing discrimination based on looks. [1]

The term later spread into university and media usage in the 1990s. Critics at the time, such as columnist Joan Beck in 1991, argued that the growing list of discrimination categories was becoming unwieldy. [1]

Research summarised on Wikipedia includes a 1998 study by Alan Slater and colleagues reporting that newborns a few hours old preferred attractive faces, which some authors read as evidence that part of the bias is innate. Eagly and colleagues (1991) described a 'what is beautiful is good' stereotype in which attractive people are rated somewhat more positively. [1]

Field experiments with fictitious résumés have reported callback advantages for attractive applicants: 36 percent more in an Argentine study (López Bóo and colleagues, 2013) and 82 percent more in a Peruvian study (Galarza and Yamada, 2017). An Israeli study (Ruffle and Shtudiner, 2015) found an advantage for attractive men but not for women. [1]

Estimates of pay effects vary. Tietje and Cresap (2005) cited a wage penalty of 7 to 9 percent for the least attractive workers and a premium of about 5 percent for the most attractive third. A 2019 study by Stinebrickner and colleagues reported that beauty premiums depend on whether appearance could affect productivity, such as in jobs with heavy interpersonal contact. [1]
A 2024 study in Behavioral Sciences examined how a 'lookism climate' and workplace incivility relate to career outcomes among employees. [6]
A longitudinal study of emerging adults in South Korea reported an association between perceived appearance discrimination and lower self-rated health. [7]

A 2024 critical ethnography in Iranian intensive care units described ageism and lookism as stereotypes contributing to health disparities between patients. [8] A 2026 philosophy paper discusses 'aesthetic injustice' in healthcare, in testimonial and hermeneutical forms. [5]

Tietje and Cresap (2005), in a paper titled 'Is Lookism Unjust?', argued that appearance preferences may be a biological adaptation, that no clear model of injustice exists, and that policy remedies are hard to justify. Others, such as Michelangelo Signorile (1997), have compared appearance hierarchies in some communities to racism or sexism. [1]

Legally, the United States once had 'ugly laws' barring people with visible disfigurements from public places until the 1970s. Today no US federal law prohibits appearance discrimination, though a few cities do, and the EEOC treats extreme obesity as a disability under the ADA in some cases. Belgium's anti-discrimination law of 10 May 2007 covers physical or genetic characteristics. [1]

A 2025 paper in Sociology of Health and Illness analysed 8,072 comments on a looksmaxxing forum reported to have around 6 million unique visitors per month. The authors describe users applying a 'hegemonic masculine gaze' to critique men's faces and bodies, and discuss how the community's health advice and self-improvement framing can affect men's health. [4]

On looksmax.org, users discuss lookism as a lived experience. One thread asks what people do once they are aware of how much looks affect treatment, and others describe frustration over appearance and neurodivergence in workplaces. Posters commonly say that the proverb that only inner qualities matter does not match their experience. [2][9]
Researchers reviewing the wider incel phenomenon note appearance-based beliefs as part of its ideology, alongside mental-health burdens. [10]

No clinical trials of lookism itself have been found, since it is a social phenomenon rather than a treatment. Observational and qualitative studies relevant to it include a Korean cohort analysis linking perceived appearance discrimination with self-rated health [7], an ethnography of lookism in intensive care [8], and a study of social appearance anxiety mediating the link between Instagram social comparison and acceptance of cosmetic surgery [11].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, lookism is discussed both as a description of how society treats people and as a source of distress, with threads about workplace treatment, neurodiversity and living in a high-appearance-pressure culture. [2][9]
